summary: Lists the IANA registries that make up the Internet Numbers Registry System, a companion to RFC 7020, which explains how that system is used to distribute AS numbers and global unicast IP address space.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of the official books where Internet address numbers are kept. It points to the exact books that count as part of the system.

questions: which iana registries are internet numbers registries
what is the internet numbers registry system
which iana registries track ip addresses
what are special purpose as numbers
subtitle: The official registries that track Internet address space allocations.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs central registries to manage and track the allocation of autonomous system numbers and IP address space globally.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7249 identifies three IANA registries that form the Internet Numbers Registry System: one for AS numbers and two for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: The registries define how globally unique address space is allocated, what is reserved for special purposes, and which values are open for allocation by regional authorities.

today: RFC 7249 is an Informational document published in May 2014. It has been updated by RFC 9812, which modernizes the registries. RFC 7249 itself remains the published specification of the core Internet Numbers Registry System at the time it was written.

sections.title: What the Internet Numbers Registry System Is
sections.content:
RFC 7249 is a short companion to RFC 7020, which explains how the Internet Numbers Registry System distributes autonomous system (AS) numbers and globally unique IP address space. This document identifies exactly which registries are part of that system.

The Internet Numbers Registry System is a coordination of IANA registries and regional Internet registries (RIRs) that allocate network resources according to policies developed by the RIRs. The three registries at the heart of the system track AS numbers, IPv4 addresses, and IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Numbers Registry System is the official record of who gets what numbers and addresses. This document says which record books are part of that official system.

sections.title: The Three Core Registries
sections.content:
Three IANA registries make up the Internet Numbers Registry System. However, each registry includes both allocated space and reserved special-purpose values, and the special-purpose values do not go through the Internet Numbers Registry System.

The three registries are: the Autonomous System (AS) Numbers registry, the IANA IPv4 Address Space Registry, and the IPv6 Global Unicast Address Assignments registry. Each handles the allocation of non-reserved space and maintains a registry of reserved values that serve specific purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three main record books: one for AS numbers, one for IPv4 addresses, and one for IPv6 addresses. Each has both a list of numbers given out and a list of numbers saved for special uses.

sections.title: Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content:
Historically, there are both 16-bit and 32-bit AS numbers, though the 16-bit AS numbers are simply the first 65,536 values of the 32-bit space (0 through 65535). The Internet Numbers Registry System handles allocation of all non-reserved AS numbers through the RIRs according to their policies.

Some AS numbers are reserved for special purposes: AS 0 is reserved, AS 23456 is used for AS number translation in RFC 6793, ranges like 64496-64511 and 64512-65534 are for documentation and private use respectively, and very large ranges such as 4200000000 to 4294967294 are also reserved for private use.
sections.plainLanguage: Every network on the Internet can have an AS number that tells other networks how to reach it. Some AS numbers are kept aside for special uses like examples in documentation.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Address Space
sections.content:
The Internet Numbers Registry System handles allocation of globally unique unicast IP addresses in both IPv4 and IPv6. For IPv4, both allocated and reserved special-purpose addresses are tracked in the IANA registry.

For IPv6, about 7/8ths of the entire address space was reserved by the IETF for future global unicast use. The remaining unicast space is allocated through the Internet Numbers Registry System. Like IPv4, special-purpose IPv6 addresses are reserved and recorded separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Most IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are given out following rules, but some are saved for special purposes like testing or private networks.

sections.title: Reserved and Special-Purpose Values
sections.content:
RFC 7249 explicitly establishes an IANA registry for special-purpose AS numbers. Future additions to this registry require IETF Review as defined in RFC 5226. Once a reservation is approved by the IETF, it is recorded in the special-purpose AS numbers registry with a reference to the RFC that documents it.

Similarly, special-purpose IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are maintained in separate IANA registries, each documented by approved RFCs. This separation ensures that the allocation system never hands out reserved numbers, and administrators know which values are reserved and why.
sections.plainLanguage: When the Internet needs to save some numbers for special uses, that decision goes through an official process and gets written down in a special list.
